name: Umar Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Umar, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I head up purchasing at Kestrel Supply, a builders' merchant wholesaler: timber, tiles, plumbing fittings, insulation, all sold to about 900 small contractors. My day starts on a call with a sawmill about delivery slots, then I go through quotes from tile makers abroad, and after lunch I'm usually in a meeting about stock levels with the sales side. I like the puzzle of getting the right goods in at the right price before a building boom or slump. What wears me out is currency swings and ships that turn up two weeks late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. I use the chatbot now and then for supplier emails, and it saves ten minutes here and there, not more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's a useful assistant and nothing more, and the team shouldn't panic or get carried away. With friends I'd say the hype is a bit silly. I'd happily tell anyone it writes a decent first draft of a quote request.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think it's fine for me. My value is knowing which tile factory will really deliver in March, and that's built on years of trust. What nags me is the mortgage and the building cycle. If housebuilding slows, my job feels the squeeze long before any software does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, and maybe use the tool a bit more for translating supplier documents and checking contract wording. I'd keep putting aside what I can each month. I'd also ask my team to share their own small tricks every Friday, because a few good habits are worth more than a big rollout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about AI itself. I feel the normal pressure of two kids and a mortgage, but there's no new fear here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said building cycles matter more. What does a slow year do to your day-to-day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Orders drop, we sit on pallets of stock, and the owners start asking why I bought so much insulation. In 2023 we carried too much, and I got a very polite but pointed meeting about it. So I watch interest rates more than I watch AI news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And at home? You've mentioned a mortgage and savings.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have about four months of spending saved, which isn't nothing. My wife Hanne is a nurse, so she's in steady work, and that helps. If the housing market sags for a year, we'd cope, but I'd be checking our bank balance more than I'd like. That's the real pressure.

say: I'd say it's a useful **assistant** and nothing more.
With friends I'd call the hype **a bit silly**, though it writes good first drafts.
think: My value is knowing which **tile factory** will really deliver, built on years of trust.
The **building cycle** and mortgage worry me more than any software.
do: Use the tool more for **translating** supplier documents and checking contracts.
Keep putting money aside, and have the team share **small tricks** each Friday.
feel: Calm about AI; the normal **pressure** of two kids and a mortgage remains.
S0.quote: If the housing market sags for a year, we'd cope, but I'd be checking our bank balance more than I'd like.
fieldNote: He treats AI as a **minor tool** and measures his risk by housing cycles instead.
Dry humour and **specific memory** (the overstocked year) make him sound lived-in.
His wife's **nursing job** is a real source of household steadiness.

steps.text: Use the chatbot to translate supplier documents and check contract wording
Hold a Friday session where the team shares AI tricks
Set aside a fixed sum each month toward the cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we're talking. Buying, planning and answering customers are literally my department.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's pick two or three jobs and let software do them properly, and measure the result. I'd tell the team it's fine to experiment. With friends I'd say companies should share the gains, not just cut headcount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think purchasing gets smaller. The routine reordering, the price comparison, the chasing of late deliveries, all that goes to software first. A team of eight might become five. I'd likely stay as the person who handles the relationships and the exceptions, but I'm not certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get ahead of it. I'd propose a pilot where the system handles repeat orders for our 200 most common items, and I'd sit on the project so I know how it works. I'd also push for the company to retrain the people who lose routine tasks. And I'd put an extra 300 a month into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but active. I'd rather be the one pushing the change than the one it lands on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd lead the pilot. What would worry you about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd be helping design the thing that makes my own team smaller. I'd have to be honest with my buyers, Marta and Joel, about that. If I hide it, I'd lose their trust, and in my job trust is most of the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marta and Joel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the routine part is going to software, and I'd offer them the supplier-relationship work and the training that goes with it. I'd rather tell my team the truth on Monday than have them find out from a spreadsheet on Friday. I think people can take bad news better than surprises.

say: I'd say pick **two or three jobs**, let software do them well, and measure it.
With friends I'd say companies should **share the gains**, not only cut headcount.
think: I think purchasing gets **smaller**: reordering and price checks go first.
I'd likely stay as the person who handles **relationships** and exceptions, but I'm not sure.
do: Propose a **pilot** for repeat orders on our 200 most common items.
Push the company to **retrain** those who lose routine tasks.
Add about **300 a month** to savings.
feel: **Anxious** but active; he'd rather push the change than be hit by it.
S1.quote: I'd rather tell my team the truth on Monday than have them find out from a spreadsheet on Friday.
fieldNote: He chooses to **lead the change** to keep some control, a clear steady-adapter move.
Honesty with his team is a **principle**, not a tactic.
His anxiety is about team size and his **own place**, not the tools.

steps.text: Pilot automatic reordering for the 200 most common items
Press the company to fund retraining for buyers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's quick. Quicker than I'd like to think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is bigger than any one company and governments have to move now: income support, retraining money and rules on who owns the gains. I'd probably join a letter to our regional representative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job goes, or turns into one person checking a machine's buying. Everything I do is thinking work: reading markets, comparing offers, negotiating. The robots arriving three years later don't matter for me, but they matter for my customers, the builders, and eventually for the whole building trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push our savings up hard, maybe cut to the bone for a year. I'd ask Hanne, my wife, to talk about whether she could take extra nursing shifts, because her work isn't touched first. I'd also look for work in the field that needs people: site supply coordination, or maybe a role in a trade association.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken. I'd think about my kids in the evening and not say much. But I'm also curious, so the feeling isn't purely fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change compared with the longer versions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's about my son. Elias would be 14, picking subjects at school. I'd be changing careers and helping him choose at the same time. With a longer runway I could do these one at a time. In two years they're stacked on top of each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd write to your representative. What would you ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real safety net before the layoffs, not after. If the state waits until my industry is already empty, the help comes too late for families like mine. Paid retraining, a bridge income, and rules so firms can't just keep all the savings.

say: I'd say governments must move now on **income support** and retraining.
I'd join a **letter** to our regional representative.
think: I think my job goes or becomes **one person** checking a machine's buying.
Robots later don't matter to me, but they matter to my **customers**, the builders.
do: Push savings up hard and **cut spending** for a year.
Ask my wife about extra **nursing shifts**, since her work isn't hit first.
Look for work needing people, like **site coordination** or a trade body.
feel: **Shaken**, quiet in the evenings, but also curious about what's possible.
S2.quote: If the state waits until my industry is already empty, the help comes too late for families like mine.
fieldNote: He expects the job to **go or shrink**; he states it without drama.
He separates **family planning** from career change, and the stacking is the pain.
He turns to **politics** and a safety-net argument early.

steps.text: Cut spending hard for a year and raise monthly savings
Look for site supply coordination or trade body roles
Write to our regional representative demanding paid retraining
Ask my wife to add extra nursing shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd treat that as a real countdown, but one with room to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to retrain and rebuild if we start now, and I'd tell the team to use the time. I'd want the company to publish its plan so nobody is guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd expect to be fine for two or three years, then watch my role shrink. I wouldn't wait for that. I'd rather move into something that benefits from the change than sit and be reduced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn to use the AI planning tools in depth within the first year, and become the person who knows them. I'd take a part-time course in supply-chain analytics. I'd also raise the cushion to six months. Hanne and I would talk about the house, whether we'd trade down if we had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though there's time to act, and I like having something to do about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd become the person who knows the tools. What does that look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run the pilot, document where it fails, and teach the others. I'd also keep my supplier relationships alive, because machines can optimise, but someone still has to say sorry to a sawmill when we cancel an order. That judgement part is what I'd protect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the house conversation with Hanne?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd look at our mortgage and what a smaller place would free up. We aren't selling anything yet, we just agree on a number. If my income dropped, we've agreed the house goes before the kids' school activities do. It's a hard conversation but I'd rather have it early.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to retrain if we start now.
I'd want the company to **publish its plan** so nobody is guessing.
think: I'd expect to be fine for two or three years, then watch the role **shrink**.
I'd rather move into something that **benefits** from the change.
do: Learn the AI planning tools **in depth** in the first year.
Raise the cushion to **six months** and discuss trading down.
feel: **Anxious**, yet there's time and something to do about it.
S3.quote: If my income dropped, we've agreed the house goes before the kids' school activities do.
fieldNote: His **steady** adaptability shows: he acts early but only once the plan is clear.
He protects the **human judgement** part of buying, like apologising to a sawmill.
Family and house trade-offs are agreed **before** any crisis.

steps.text: Learn the AI planning tools in depth and teach the team
Take a part-time supply chain analytics course
Raise the cushion to six months of spending

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. By then Elias is 22 and Noor is 19. That's a different life stage entirely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets people change careers properly, and I'd encourage the younger buyers to start now. I'd also say governments should use the time, not coast through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel okay. I'd have time to move laterally into something I like, and my kids will be nearly grown, which makes risk easier to carry. I'm more worried that society will waste ten years arguing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning the tools at a steady pace, build savings, and consider a master's module in operations. I'd probably also start mentoring younger buyers on how to deal with people, which won't be automated early. I'd look at whether our firm will fund any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. It's the version that feels like planning, not surviving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have done by year five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mortgage balance well down, savings at half a year or more, and a role that isn't just buying. Maybe supplier development, working with factories on quality and sustainability. In ten years I'd like to be the person who visits the factories, not the person who clicks the reorder button.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in the longer timeline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Complacency, mostly. Ten years makes people say 'later'. I'd have to be disciplined, set up an annual check on my skills and money. And watch my firm, because a company that ignores the warning could fold before the technology arrives.

say: I'd say a **decade** lets people change careers properly.
I'd urge governments to **use the time**, not coast.
think: Privately I feel okay; I'd have time to move **sideways** into work I like.
I worry society will **waste** ten years arguing.
do: Keep learning the tools at a **steady pace** and build savings.
Look at an **operations** module, and mentor younger buyers on people skills.
feel: Fairly **calm**; it feels like planning, not surviving.
S4.quote: In ten years I'd like to be the person who visits the factories, not the person who clicks the reorder button.
fieldNote: He imagines a **supplier-visiting** role, which suits his interest in the human side.
The risk he names is **complacency**, not the technology.
His stability comes from **kids nearly grown** by that time.

steps.text: Study an operations management module over two winters
Mentor younger buyers on negotiation and supplier visits
Build savings to half a year of spending

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. Not because I'm sure it happens, but because it stacks everything: career, kids' choices, mortgage. What would help is a bridge income, paid retraining, and my company telling us early what it plans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that people like me don't feel like victims. I'm not scared of the machine itself. I'm scared of the way companies will use it to save money while they tell us it's an opportunity.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of the machine itself. I'm scared of the way companies will use it to save money while they tell us it's an opportunity.
portrait: Umar Jensen, 43, heads purchasing at a **builders' merchant**, with a nurse wife and two school-age children.
Progressive and steady: uses AI **now and then** and acts early once a plan looks proven.
Has about **four months** saved and a mortgage; he judges risk by the housing cycle more than by AI.
Calm in the plateau and the ten-year world, and **alarmed** by the 2028 case.
Blames **firms** that bank the savings, and turns to politics and honest talk with his team.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario stacks his career, kids' choices and mortgage at once.
whatWouldHelp: His company **telling staff early** what it plans.
